issues.issue: Husband treated as receiving $35,999 of social security benefits for 2014 (incl. $7,723 workers' compensation offset)
issues.lean: socialSecurity input; the §86(d)(3) characterisation is made outside the framework (input-level)
issues.diagnosis: Framework takes benefits as a number; it has no §86(d)(3) workers'-compensation-offset rule, so the holding is an input, not a computation. Taxable amount not stated by the court.
issues.snippet: Under section 86 petitioner husband is taxed as if he received $35,999 in Social Security disability benefits for 2014.

issues.issue: 2017+ repayment of $49,170 does not reduce 2014 income
issues.lean: not modelled (year of inclusion / claim of right)
issues.diagnosis: Timing-of-inclusion rule for a cash-method taxpayer; framework has no multi-year or §1341 model.
issues.snippet: Petitioners' repayments in 2017 of benefits received in 2014 do not affect their 2014 tax liability.

issues.diagnosis: Rerun 57b55431cca: 2014 now runs, but the opinion states no other income, deductions or the return as filed, so the 9,717 deficiency cannot be recomputed (with benefits alone provisional income 18,000 < 32,000 gives 0 taxable). Arithmetic: 85% x 35,999 = 30,599; 9,717/30,599 = 31.8% average rate implies other taxable income near the 2014 MFJ 28%/33% boundary (226,850), roughly 219,000. Inference only.
issues.snippet: Respondent determined that petitioners had an income tax deficiency of $9,717 for taxable year 2014.
Respondent concedes that petitioners are not liable for the accuracy-related penalty under sec. 6662(a).

notes: Rerun 2c5b6354943: runs (exit 0, no expected items). Deficiency not encodable: other income absent from the opinion. The framework now has a sec. 86(e) field (ssLumpSums), but it is not used here: the court did not discuss the election, and neither 2013 modified income nor 2014 other income is in the opinion (SSA-1099 shows $18,599 attributable to 2013), so nothing about it can be computed or compared.
